Empirical Research Plan  

------------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Identification Strategy  
------------------------------------------------------------------  
a) Incidence on earnings / employment / seasonality (micro WA data)  
 • Difference-in-Differences (firm-by-time) combined with an event-study on quarters.  
  – Cross-sectional “dose” comes from the tax rate each firm is suddenly assigned for 1985, which is a deterministic function of its 1981-83 layoff record and therefore predetermined at the moment of the reform.  
  – Time variation comes from the sharp introduction of experience-rating on 1 Jan 1985.  

b) Effects on UI claims, denial rates, etc. (state panel)  
 • Two-way-fixed-effects DID with a continuous treatment: each state-quarter is weighted by the statutory average marginal UI tax cost (AMTC).  
 • Event-study around Washington’s 1985 reform (WA vs. synthetic control from OR, ID, and the rest of the country) to show parallel pre-trends.  
 • A triple-difference for seasonality: (high-season – low-season months) × (post – pre) × (WA – controls).  

Both designs exploit credible policy-induced exogenous variation and can be implemented with standard panel methods.  

------------------------------------------------------------------  
2. Treatment and Control  
------------------------------------------------------------------  
a) Firm-level incidence design  
 • Treatment variable: statutory UI payroll tax rate τi,1985 assigned to firm i.  
  – Operationalised either as the discrete rate (e.g. 0.6 % … 5.4 %) or as the change Δτi = τi,1985 – 3.3 % (the common 1984 rate).  
 • Treated vs. control: all firms are “exposed”, but the treatment intensity differs. We therefore estimate a dose-response (continuous DID).  
 • Treatment timing: Post = 1 for quarters ≥ 1985 Q1; pre-period = 1984 Q3–Q4 (we drop Q1-Q2 1984 to avoid announcement/anticipation).  

b) State-level UI-claims design  
 • Treatment variable: AMTCst (= expected extra tax dollars per $100 of wages caused by an additional layoff in state s at time t).  
 • Control group: states with unchanged or smoothly evolving AMTC serve as counterfactuals; WA’s 1985 jump is the focal shock.  
 • Event date: 1985 Q1.  

------------------------------------------------------------------  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
------------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel trends: absent the reform, outcomes would have evolved similarly across firms with different predetermined benefit ratios and across WA and comparison states.  
 • Plausibility: tax assignment is based on 1981-83 layoffs, not on future growth expectations; OR and ID share labour-market trends with WA.  

A2. No simultaneous confounders hitting treated units differentially at the same time (e.g., industry-specific shocks correlated with layoff history).  
 • Mitigation: include firm, industry×quarter, and county×quarter fixed effects.  

A3. No anticipatory behaviour strongly affecting the pre-period (firms only learned final rates in March 1984, leaving very little time to react before Q3 1984).  

A4. Stable unit treatment values (no spillovers across firms or states strong enough to bias results). WA is a small share of national employment, so cross-state spillovers should be limited.  

------------------------------------------------------------------  
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies  
------------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Differential pre-trends by layoff history.  
 • Remedy: event-study coefficients for seven pre-quarters; discard outcomes if significant pre-trends; re-weight using entropy balancing on 1982-84 trends.  

T2. Industry-specific shocks coinciding with reform (e.g., aerospace slump).  
 • Remedy: industry×time fixed effects and a robustness check dropping the most cyclically sensitive 2-digit SICs.  

T3. Firms manipulate layoffs in 1984 Q4 to influence 1985 rates.  
 • Remedy: verify that the benefit-ratio formula freezes experience through 1983, making manipulation impossible; additionally, estimate results excluding 1984 Q4.  

------------------------------------------------------------------  
5. R Code Outline (Incidence specification shown)  
------------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# Packages
library(data.table)    # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)        # high-dim FE regressions
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data -----------------------------------------------------------
micro <- fread("washington_micro.csv")   # quarter-level person-firm data

# 2. Variable construction ----------------------------------------------
micro[, post := (year >= 1985)]
micro[, tax_change := tax_rate_1985 - 0.033]     # 3.3% baseline
micro[, quarter_id := paste0(year,"Q",quarter)]
micro[, ln_earn := log(earnings + 1)]            # avoid log(0)

# Collapse to firm×quarter to study employment levels
firm_q <- micro[, .(
  emp = uniqueN(person_id),
  avg_earn = mean(earnings)
), by = .(firm_id, tax_change, industry2, county, quarter_id, year, quarter, post)]

# 3. Main DID regression -------------------------------------------------
# Outcome 1: log average earnings
res1 <- feols(log(avg_earn) ~ post*tax_change | 
              firm_id + industry2^quarter_id + county^quarter_id, 
              data = firm_q, cluster = ~industry2)
summary(res1)

# Event-study (leads/lags)
firm_q[, rel_q := as.integer(factor(quarter_id, 
                      levels = sort(unique(quarter_id))) ) - 
                      which(quarter_id == "1985Q1"), by = firm_id]
res_es <- feols(log(avg_earn) ~ i(rel_q, tax_change, ref = -1) |
                firm_id + industry2^quarter_id + county^quarter_id,
                data = firm_q, cluster = ~industry2)
iplot(res_es)

# 4. Robustness: re-weight by inverse propensity for tax_change ----------
# (here a simple linear prediction on 1982-84 growth)
prefit <- feols(tax_change ~ g_8284_emp + g_8284_wage + industry2,
                data = unique(firm_q[, .(firm_id, tax_change, g_8284_emp, g_8284_wage, industry2)]))
firm_q[, w := 1 / exp(predict(prefit, newdata = .))]
res_rb <- feols(log(avg_earn) ~ post*tax_change | 
                firm_id + industry2^quarter_id + county^quarter_id, 
                data = firm_q, weight = ~w, cluster = ~industry2)
summary(res_rb)
```  
(An analogous script would run the state-level panel using AMTCst as treatment.)  

------------------------------------------------------------------  
6. Expected Results  
------------------------------------------------------------------  
Theory: In a competitive labour market with rigid total compensation, a 1 pp rise in payroll tax should lower workers’ after-tax earnings roughly one-for-one in the long run, but with partial shifting in the short run.  
 • Earnings: β ≈ -0.6 to ‑0.8 (i.e., 60-80 % incidence on workers within a year).  
 • Employment level: small negative effect, perhaps ‑0.2 % per ppt.  
 • Seasonality: experience-rating should reduce seasonal layoffs, lowering the within-year employment range by 2-3 %.  
 • UI claims: WA’s reform should cut initial claims by 10-15 % and reduce denial rates because marginal claims fall.  

------------------------------------------------------------------  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Difference-in-Differences)  
C1 Parallel pre-trends ……………………………………… 1  
C2 No contemporaneous shocks ………………………… 0.5  
C3 No anticipation ………………………………………… 1  
C4 Stable composition of units ………………………… 1  
C5 No interference / spillovers ………………………… 0.5  
 Total = 4/5 ⇒ generally credible but must document robustness.
